note: Diagnostic questions. The correct choice is listed first and choices are shuffled when shown. 'I don't know yet' is added by the app.

questions.stem: A vector $\vec A$ of length 10 lies in the $x$-$y$ plane at $30^\circ$ above the $+x$ axis. Its components $(A_x, A_y)$ are:
$\vec a=(1,2,2)$ and $\vec b=(2,0,1)$. What is $\vec a\cdot\vec b$?
questions.why: $1\cdot2+2\cdot0+2\cdot1=4$; a dot product is a number, not a vector.

questions.stem: What is the component of $\vec a=(3,4,0)$ along the unit vector $\hat u=(0.6,\,0.8,\,0)$?
questions.why: $\vec a\cdot\hat u=3(0.6)+4(0.8)=5$ (here $\hat u$ points along $\vec a$).

questions.stem: $\vec a=(1,0,0)$ and $\vec b=(0,2,0)$. What is $\vec a\times\vec b$?
questions.why: $\hat x\times2\hat y=2\hat z$.

questions.stem: With right-handed axes ($\hat x$ east, $\hat y$ north, $\hat z$ up), what is $\hat z\times\hat x$?
questions.why: Cyclic order $\hat x\to\hat y\to\hat z\to\hat x$: $\hat z\times\hat x=\hat y$.

questions.stem: A vector $\vec A$ of fixed length turns about the vertical $\hat z$ axis at rate $\Omega$, keeping a fixed angle with $\hat z$. Which is true?
choices: $d\vec A/dt=\Omega\hat z\times\vec A$: horizontal, with size $\Omega$ times the horizontal part of $\vec A$
$d\vec A/dt$ is vertical because the tip circles the vertical axis
questions.why: The tip moves on a horizontal circle of radius $A_\perp$ at angular rate $\Omega$, so $d\vec A/dt=\vec\Omega\times\vec A$ with size $\Omega A_\perp$.

questions.stem: $\vec L=(3,0,4)$ turns about $\hat z$ at $\Omega=2$ rad/s. What is $|d\vec L/dt|$?
questions.why: $2\hat z\times(3,0,4)=(0,6,0)$: only the horizontal part (3) counts, $2\times3=6$.

questions.stem: $\dfrac{d}{dt}\sin\theta(t)=\ ?$
questions.why: Chain rule: $\cos\theta\cdot d\theta/dt$.

questions.stem: $\displaystyle\int_0^L x^2\,dx=\ ?$
questions.why: The antiderivative of $x^2$ is $x^3/3$.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is cut into thin rings of radius $r$ and width $dr$. The mass of one ring is:
questions.why: $dm=\sigma\cdot2\pi r\,dr$ with $\sigma=M/\pi R^2$.

questions.stem: For small $\theta$, $1-\cos\theta\approx\ ?$
questions.why: $\cos\theta\approx1-\theta^2/2$.

questions.stem: For $x\ll1$, $\sqrt{1+x}\approx\ ?$
questions.why: $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx$ with $n=\tfrac12$.

questions.stem: An angle obeys $\ddot\theta=-\dfrac{3g}{2L}\,\theta$. The angular frequency of its oscillations is:
questions.why: $\ddot\theta=-\omega^2\theta$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{3g/2L}$.

questions.stem: At a point on the $+x$ axis, which way does $\hat\phi$ point?
questions.why: $\hat\phi$ points in the direction of increasing angle, counterclockwise seen from above.

questions.stem: In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi,z)$, $\hat z\times\hat r=\ ?$
questions.why: $(\hat r,\hat\phi,\hat z)$ is right-handed, so $\hat z\times\hat r=\hat\phi$.

questions.stem: $\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&3&1\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\ ?$
Let $\hat e_3=\cos\theta\,\hat x+\sin\theta\,\hat z$ and $\hat e_2=-\sin\theta\,\hat x+\cos\theta\,\hat z$. The components of $\hat x$ along $(\hat e_3,\hat e_2)$ are:
questions.why: $\hat x\cdot\hat e_3=\cos\theta$ and $\hat x\cdot\hat e_2=-\sin\theta$.

questions.stem: The eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ are:
questions.why: $(3-\lambda)^2-1=0$ gives $\lambda=4,2$.

questions.stem: For $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, which vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 4?
questions.why: $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Which formula for a top's precession rate $\Omega$ has the right units? ($M$ mass, $g$ gravity, $\ell$ length, $I$ moment of inertia, $\omega$ spin rate)
questions.why: $Mg\ell$ is a torque (kg m²/s²) and $I\omega$ is angular momentum (kg m²/s), so their ratio is 1/s.

questions.stem: A block slides down a frictionless incline of angle $\theta$. Someone proposes $a=g\sin\theta\cos\theta$. Which check shows it is wrong?
choices: At $\theta=90^\circ$ it gives 0, but a vertical 'incline' is free fall with $a=g$
At $\theta=0$ it gives 0, which is wrong
No limiting case can test it
questions.why: The correct answer is $g\sin\theta$; the $\theta\to90^\circ$ limit exposes the extra $\cos\theta$.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block is pushed with 10 N across a floor against 4 N of kinetic friction. Its acceleration is:
A ball on a string swings in a horizontal circle (a conical pendulum). Which forces act on the ball?
choices: Gravity, tension and a centripetal force
Gravity, tension and a centrifugal force
questions.why: Centripetal is the name of the net inward force (here a part of the tension), not an extra force.

questions.stem: A point moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at $\omega=4$ rad/s. Its acceleration is:
questions.why: $a=r\omega^2=0.5\times16=8$ m/s², pointing inward.

questions.stem: Two skaters, 60 kg and 40 kg, push off from rest. The 60 kg skater moves at 2 m/s. The other moves at:
questions.why: Momentum stays zero: $60\times2=40v$.

questions.stem: A 1 kg mass is at $x=0$ and a 3 kg mass at $x=4$ m. Where is the center of mass?
For $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-\tfrac12kx^2$, the Euler–Lagrange equation is:
questions.why: $\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot x)=-kx$.

questions.stem: For $L=\tfrac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2)-V(r)$, which quantity is conserved because $\theta$ is cyclic?
questions.why: $\partial L/\partial\dot\theta=mr^2\dot\theta$ is conserved.

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m$ moves with velocity $v\hat y$ along the line $x=d$ (in the $x$-$y$ plane). Its angular momentum about the origin is:
choices: $mvd\,\hat z$, the same at every point of the line
questions.why: $\vec r\times m\vec v=(d,y,0)\times(0,mv,0)=mvd\,\hat z$.

questions.stem: A uniform disk (mass $M$, radius $R$) spins at $\omega$ about the perpendicular axis through its center. Its angular momentum is:
questions.why: $L=I\omega$ with $I=\tfrac12MR^2$.

questions.stem: A thin ring (mass $M$, radius $R$) spins at $\omega$ about its central perpendicular axis. Its kinetic energy is:
questions.why: $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ with $I=MR^2$.

questions.stem: A uniform disk (mass $M$) rolls without slipping at speed $v$. Its total kinetic energy is:
questions.why: $\tfrac12Mv^2+\tfrac12(\tfrac12MR^2)(v/R)^2=\tfrac34Mv^2$.

questions.stem: A uniform rod (mass $M$, length $\ell$) has $I_{CM}=M\ell^2/12$. Its moment of inertia about one end is:
A uniform disk (mass $M$, radius $R$) rotates about an axis perpendicular to it through a point on its rim. $I=\ ?$
questions.why: $\tfrac12MR^2+MR^2$.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a uniform disk (mass $M$, radius $R$) about a diameter is:
questions.why: $I_x+I_y=I_z=\tfrac12MR^2$ and $I_x=I_y$.

questions.stem: A rigid body is forced to rotate about the fixed $z$ axis. Which is always true?
choices: $\vec L$ is parallel to $\vec\omega$ for every body
questions.why: Only the $z$ component is guaranteed; a lopsided body has sideways $\vec L$ components (which is why axles feel wobbling torques).

questions.stem: Same mass $M$ and radius $R$: which has the largest moment of inertia about its central axis?
questions.why: Hoop $MR^2$ > disk $\tfrac12MR^2$ > sphere $\tfrac25MR^2$: all the hoop's mass is far out.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about a diameter is:
questions.why: Solid sphere $\tfrac25MR^2$; the thin shell is $\tfrac23MR^2$.

questions.stem: Using rings, $I_{disk}=\displaystyle\int_0^R r^2\,\frac{2Mr}{R^2}\,dr=\ ?$
questions.why: $\frac{2M}{R^2}\cdot\frac{R^4}{4}=\tfrac12MR^2$.

questions.stem: A massless rod of length $\ell$ has a point mass $m$ at each end. Its moment about a perpendicular axis through the rod's center is:
questions.why: $2\times m(\ell/2)^2$.

questions.stem: A force $F\hat y$ acts at the point $d\hat x$. Its torque about the origin is:
questions.why: $d\hat x\times F\hat y=dF\,\hat z$.

questions.stem: About which points can you always use $\vec\tau=d\vec L/dt$?
choices: A fixed point, or the center of mass even if it accelerates
Only points where the net force is zero
questions.why: The CM works because the fictitious force in its frame acts at the CM and has no torque about it.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius $R$ rolls without slipping at speed $v$. How fast is the top of the wheel moving?
questions.why: The contact point is at rest; the top is twice as far from it: $v+\omega R=2v$.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping across flat ground at constant speed. The friction force from the ground is:
questions.why: Nothing needs to change the motion, so no friction is needed (ignoring rolling resistance).

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere rolls without slipping down an incline of angle $\theta$. Its acceleration is:
questions.why: $g\sin\theta/(1+\tfrac25)$.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length $\ell$ swings about one end. Its small-oscillation angular frequency is:
questions.why: $\omega^2=Mgd/I=Mg(\ell/2)/(M\ell^2/3)=3g/2\ell$.

questions.stem: A ball hits and sticks to a rod hanging from a frictionless pivot. Through the collision, what is conserved?
choices: Linear momentum of ball plus rod
Angular momentum about the ball's starting point
questions.why: The pivot's large impulsive force has no torque about the pivot, but it does change linear momentum.

questions.stem: A free uniform stick (mass $M$, length $\ell$) at rest gets an impulse $J$ perpendicular to it at one end. Right after, $V_{CM}$ and $\omega$ are:
questions.why: $MV=J$ and $I_{CM}\omega=J\ell/2$ with $I_{CM}=M\ell^2/12$.

questions.stem: You hold a uniform stick at one end. Where should a ball hit it so your hand feels no jolt?
questions.why: There the CM's forward jump exactly cancels the backward rotation at your hand.

questions.stem: Which describes the motion of any rigid body at a given instant?
choices: The velocity of any one chosen point plus a rotation $\vec\omega$ about it; $\vec\omega$ is the same whichever point you choose
A rotation about the center of mass only
A pure translation, if you pick the right point
A rotation whose $\vec\omega$ depends on the point you choose
questions.why: Morin 9.1.1: translation of a point plus rotation; the angular velocity doesn't depend on the chosen point.

questions.stem: A body rotates about the origin with $\vec\omega=\omega\hat z$. The velocity of the body point at $(0,R,0)$ is:
questions.why: $\omega\hat z\times R\hat y=-\omega R\,\hat x$.

questions.stem: A wheel spins at $\omega'$ about its axle direction $\hat e_3$ (relative to the axle), while the axle turns about the vertical at $\Omega\hat z$. The wheel's angular velocity is:
questions.why: Angular velocities add as vectors.

questions.stem: A cone rolls without slipping on a table with its tip fixed. Its angular velocity points:
choices: Along the line where the cone touches the table
Along the cone's own symmetry axis
Horizontally, perpendicular to the contact line
questions.why: Every point on the contact line is momentarily at rest, so it is the instantaneous axis.

questions.stem: Two points $O$ and $P$ of a rigid body are momentarily at rest. Then:
choices: $\vec\omega$ lies along the line $OP$ (or is zero)
questions.why: $\vec v_P=\vec\omega\times\vec{OP}=0$ requires $\vec\omega\parallel\vec{OP}$.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius $r$ on an axle pivoted at ground level rolls without slipping (the axle is tilted so the rim touches the ground). Its contact point is a distance $R$ from the pivot and circles it at rate $\Omega$. The wheel's spin relative to the axle is:
questions.why: No slipping: the rim speed $r\omega'$ matches the ground's speed $R\Omega$ under the contact point, in the frame turning with the axle.

questions.stem: A cone of half-angle $\alpha$ rolls without slipping on a table, tip fixed, its axis circling the vertical at rate $\Omega$. How fast does it spin relative to a frame turning with its axis?
questions.why: The axis is tilted $\alpha$ above the table. $\vec\omega=\Omega\hat z+\omega'\hat e_3$ must lie along the horizontal contact line, so $\omega'\sin\alpha=\Omega$.

questions.stem: A dumbbell (two equal masses at the ends of a rod through the origin) is tilted from the $z$ axis and spun about the $z$ axis. Which is true?
choices: $\vec L$ has a horizontal part, so it is not parallel to $\vec\omega$
questions.why: For a mass at $(a,0,b)$: $\vec r\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r)$ has an $x$ part $-ab\,\omega$, so $\vec L$ tilts away from $\hat z$.

questions.stem: In units of $ma^2$, $\mathbf I=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&-1\\0&2&0\\-1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec\omega=\omega\hat z$. Then $\vec L$ is:
questions.why: $\mathbf I\vec\omega$ is the third column times $\omega$.

questions.stem: A point mass $m$ sits at $(a,a,0)$. What is $I_{xy}$ about the origin?
questions.why: $I_{xy}=-\sum m\,xy=-ma^2$.

questions.stem: The same point mass $m$ at $(a,a,0)$: what is $I_{zz}$ about the origin?
$\vec\omega=(0,0,\omega)$ and $\vec L=(-\omega,0,\omega)\,ma^2$. The kinetic energy is:
questions.why: $\tfrac12\vec\omega\cdot\vec L=\tfrac12\omega\cdot\omega\,ma^2$.

questions.stem: A body's CM is at $\vec R$ moving with $\vec V$, and the body rotates with $\vec\omega$. Its angular momentum about the origin is:
questions.why: Orbital part of the CM plus spin about the CM.

questions.stem: A body's CM is at $\vec R=(0,0,d)$ from the origin. Compare $I_{zz}$ about the origin with $I_{zz}$ about the CM:
questions.why: The shift is along $z$: $M(R^2-R_z^2)=0$. Both $z$ axes are the same line.

questions.stem: With the same shift $\vec R=(0,0,d)$, $I_{xx}$ about the origin is:
What makes an axis (through a given point) a principal axis?
choices: If $\vec\omega$ points along it, $\vec L$ points along it too
It passes through the center of mass
The moment of inertia about it is the largest
questions.why: Principal axes are the eigenvectors of $\mathbf I$: $\mathbf I\vec\omega=\lambda\vec\omega$. Symmetry axes are principal, but not every principal axis is a symmetry axis.

questions.stem: Written in a basis of principal axes, the inertia tensor is:
choices: Zero except in the first row
questions.why: The principal moments sit on the diagonal.

questions.stem: A uniform disk sits on a massless axle along its symmetry axis, with a pivot at the axle's far end. Which are principal axes through the pivot?
choices: The axle, and every axis through the pivot perpendicular to it
Only axes through the disk's center
questions.why: The body is symmetric about the axle and the pivot lies on it.

questions.stem: For that disk (mass $m$, radius $r$) with the pivot a distance $\ell$ from its center, the moment about a perpendicular principal axis through the pivot is:
questions.why: A diameter's $\tfrac14mr^2$ plus the parallel-axis term $m\ell^2$.

questions.stem: In units of $ma^2$, $\mathbf I=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&0\\1&3&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$. The principal moments are:
questions.why: The $2\times2$ block gives 4 and 2; the $zz$ entry is already 2.

questions.stem: A symmetric body has moment $I_3$ about its axis $\hat e_3$ and $I$ about perpendicular axes. If $\vec\omega=\omega_3\hat e_3+\omega_2\hat e_2$, then $\vec L=$
questions.why: Each principal component of $\vec\omega$ is multiplied by its own moment.

questions.stem: A wheel spins at $\omega'$ relative to its axle $\hat e_3$ while the axle turns at $-\Omega\hat z$; $\hat e_3$ is tilted up $\theta$ from the horizontal. The total component $\omega_3$ along $\hat e_3$ is:
questions.why: $\vec\omega=-\Omega\hat z+\omega'\hat e_3$ and $\hat z\cdot\hat e_3=\sin\theta$.

questions.stem: A body at rest gets angular momentum $\vec L$ from a blow, and $\vec L$ is not along a principal axis. Right after the blow:
choices: $\vec\omega=\mathbf I^{-1}\vec L$, which is not parallel to $\vec L$
The body only starts rotating later
questions.why: Resolve $\vec L$ along the principal axes and divide each part by its own moment.

questions.stem: $\vec L$ has a vertical part $L_z$ and a horizontal part $L_\perp$, and the whole vector turns about the vertical at rate $\Omega$. Then $|d\vec L/dt|$ is:
questions.why: $\vec\Omega\times\vec L$ only sees the part of $\vec L$ perpendicular to $\vec\Omega$.

questions.stem: A gyroscope's axle is horizontal and supported at one end; it precesses steadily. Taking torques about the support point, which force(s) contribute?
choices: Only gravity, acting at the center of mass
None; torque is zero in steady precession
questions.why: The support force acts at the origin you chose, so it has no lever arm.

questions.stem: For a torque-free body with principal moments $I_1, I_2, I_3$, Euler's equation gives $\dot\omega_1=$
questions.why: $I_1\dot\omega_1+(I_3-I_2)\omega_2\omega_3=0$.

questions.stem: A book with $I_1<I_2<I_3$ is tossed spinning about one principal axis. About which one is the spin unstable?
choices: The axis with the largest moment
The axis with the smallest moment
questions.why: The tennis-racket theorem.

questions.stem: A torque-free symmetric top ($I_1=I_2=I$, $I_3$). Seen from the body, $\vec\omega$ precesses around $\hat e_3$ at:
questions.why: From Euler's equations with $\omega_3$ constant.

questions.stem: The same free top seen from the fixed frame: which vector stays fixed in space?
questions.why: No torque means constant $\vec L$; $\vec\omega$ and $\hat e_3$ circle around it.

questions.stem: In Morin's treatment of the top, which Euler angle is the tilt of the symmetry axis from the vertical?
questions.why: $\phi$ is the precession angle and $\psi$ the spin about the symmetry axis.

questions.stem: With $\theta$ measured from the vertical, the component of $\vec\omega$ along a top's symmetry axis is:
questions.why: $\dot\phi\hat z$ contributes $\dot\phi\cos\theta$ along $\hat e_3$.

questions.stem: A heavy top precesses steadily at rate $\Omega$, tilted $\theta$ from the vertical, with pivot-to-CM distance $\ell$. The exact condition is:
questions.why: Morin's torque method, with $I$ about a perpendicular axis through the pivot; the second choice is only the fast-top approximation.

questions.stem: A top is spun faster (larger $\omega_3$). Its slow precession rate:
questions.why: $\Omega\approx Mg\ell/(I_3\omega_3)$.

questions.stem: In the heavy top's Lagrangian written with Euler angles, which coordinates are cyclic?
questions.why: $L$ depends on $\theta$ but not on $\phi$ or $\psi$, giving two conserved momenta.

questions.stem: A fast top is released with its axis tilted and not precessing. Its tip mostly:
choices: Drifts sideways at about the slow precession rate while bobbing with small, fast wobbles
questions.why: That bobbing is nutation; for a fast top its frequency is about $I_3\omega_3/I$.

questions.stem: A top spinning with its axis vertical stays up (is stable) if:
questions.why: The sleeping-top condition; below it, a small tilt grows.

questions.stem: A vector in the $x$-$y$ plane is $\mathbf a=-\sqrt3\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\hat{\mathbf y}$. What are its magnitude and its direction, measured counterclockwise from the $+x$ axis?
questions.why: $a=\sqrt{3+1}=2$. $\tan\theta=a_y/a_x=1/\sqrt3$, and since both components are negative the vector is in the third quadrant, so $\theta=180^\circ+30^\circ=210^\circ$. The most tempting wrong answer is $30^\circ$, which comes from taking the arctan without checking the quadrant.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: Block A (3 kg) and block B (1 kg) touch each other on a frictionless floor. A horizontal 8 N push in the $+x$ direction acts on A, which pushes B ahead of it. What force does B exert on A?
questions.why: Both blocks have $a=8/4=2$ m/s², so A pushes B with $m_Ba=2$ N in $+x$. By the third law, B pushes back on A with 2 N in $-x$. The tempting mistake is to give the force of A on B ($+x$) instead of its reaction.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: At the top of its flight, a 2 kg shell moving horizontally at 10 m/s explodes into two 1 kg pieces. Just after the explosion, one piece is at rest. What is the velocity of the other piece just after the explosion?
choices: Undetermined, because gravity is an external force
questions.why: Gravity has no horizontal component, so horizontal momentum is conserved: $2(10)=1\cdot v$, giving $v=20$ m/s. The $10\sqrt2$ answer comes from wrongly conserving kinetic energy, and the 'undetermined' answer forgets that momentum is conserved component by component.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A 1 kg mass moving at 6 m/s approaches a 2 kg mass at rest along a line. How much of the system's lab kinetic energy is kinetic energy relative to the center of mass, $K_{CM}$?
questions.why: $u=P/M=6/3=2$ m/s, so $K_{CM}=K_{lab}-\tfrac12Mu^2=18-6=12$ J. 18 J is the whole lab kinetic energy, 6 J is the CM-motion part, and 4.5 J comes from using the plain average velocity (3 m/s) instead of the mass-weighted one.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A pendulum bob has height $y=-\ell\cos\theta(t)$, where $\ell$ is constant. What is $\ddot y$?
questions.why: $\dot y=\ell\sin\theta\,\dot\theta$. Using the product rule and chain rule gives $\ddot y=\ell(\cos\theta\,\dot\theta^2+\sin\theta\,\ddot\theta)$. The most tempting error is to treat $\dot\theta$ as constant, which drops the centripetal $\dot\theta^2$ term.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A free particle of mass $m$ moves in a plane, with $L=\tfrac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2)$ in polar coordinates. Its Euler–Lagrange equation for $\theta$, after dividing by $mr$, is:
questions.why: $\partial L/\partial\theta=0$ and $\frac{d}{dt}(mr^2\dot\theta)=m(2r\dot r\dot\theta+r^2\ddot\theta)$, which gives the Coriolis term $2\dot r\dot\theta$. The tempting mistake is to treat $r^2$ as constant inside the total time derivative, which gives $r\ddot\theta=0$.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A particle has $L=\tfrac12 m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi^2)-V(r,\theta)$. At one moment $r=a$, $\theta=90^\circ$, $\dot\phi=\omega$. Later it has $r=a$, $\theta=30^\circ$. What is $\dot\phi$ then?
questions.why: $\phi$ is cyclic, so $mr^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi$ is conserved. Since $\sin^2 30^\circ=\tfrac14$, $\dot\phi$ must become $4\omega$. The most tempting wrong answer, $\omega$, comes from treating $\dot\phi$ itself as the conserved quantity. Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin^2\theta$ gives $2\omega$, and inverting the ratio gives $\omega/4$.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A particle of mass $1$ kg is at $(x,y)=(4,3)$ m with velocity $(v_x,v_y)=(0,2)$ m/s in the plane $z=0$. What is its angular momentum about the origin, in kg·m²/s?
questions.why: $L_z=m(xv_y-yv_x)=1(4\cdot2-3\cdot0)=+8$. Reversing the cross product to $\mathbf p\times\mathbf r$ gives $-8$. Using $mrv$ with $r=5$ gives $10$, and using $y$ instead of $x$ as the lever arm gives $6$.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A uniform thin stick of mass $M$ and length $\ell$ lies in the $x$-$y$ plane. It is pivoted at one end at the origin and spins about the $z$ axis at angular speed $\omega$. What is $L_z$?
questions.why: $I_z=\int_0^\ell x^2\,(M/\ell)\,dx=M\ell^2/3$, so $L_z=\tfrac13M\ell^2\omega$. The $\tfrac1{12}$ answer uses the moment of inertia about the center instead of about the pivot. The $\tfrac14$ answer treats the stick as a point mass at its CM and drops $I^{CM}$. The last answer puts all the mass at the far end.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ ($I^{CM}=\tfrac12MR^2$) lies in the $x$-$y$ plane, with $y$ pointing up. It rolls without slipping in the $+x$ direction along the ground $y=0$ at speed $v$. What is its angular momentum about the origin, a fixed point on the ground?
questions.why: The CM term is $(\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V)_z=M(X\cdot0-R\,v)=-MRv$. The disk spins clockwise at $v/R$, so the spin term is $-\tfrac12MRv$, and the total is $-\tfrac32MRv\,\hat z$. Leaving out the CM point-mass term gives $-\tfrac12MRv$ (so does giving the spin the wrong sign). Leaving out the spin gives $-MRv$.
questions.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 answered it blind (2026-09-23)

questions.stem: A force of $2$ N in the $-\hat x$ direction acts at the point $(x,y)=(4,3)$ m. What is the torque about the origin, in N·m?
questions.why: $\tau_z=xF_y-yF_x=4\cdot0-3(-2)=+6$. The lever arm is the perpendicular distance, 3 m, from the origin to the horizontal line of action. Writing $\mathbf F\times\mathbf r$ flips the sign to $-6$. Using $x=4$ or the distance $r=5$ as the lever arm gives 8 or 10.

questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder ($I=\tfrac12MR^2$) rolls without slipping down a fixed incline of angle $\theta$. You apply $\tau=dL/dt$ about the fixed point on the incline where it touches at that instant, so $\tau=MgR\sin\theta$. What CM acceleration does this give?

questions.stem: A 1 kg ball at $\mathbf r = 0.2\,\hat{\mathbf y}$ m circles the origin clockwise, seen from above ($+z$), at 5 rad/s in the $xy$-plane. What is its angular momentum $\mathbf L$ about the origin, in kg m²/s?
questions.why: Clockwise gives $\boldsymbol\omega=-5\hat{\mathbf z}$, so $\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=+1\,\hat{\mathbf x}$ m/s and $\mathbf L=m\,\mathbf r\times\mathbf v=0.2(\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf x})=-0.2\hat{\mathbf z}$. The wrong choices come from flipping the sign (wrong hand, or computing $\mathbf p\times\mathbf r$), using $mr\omega$, or leaving out $\omega$.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass $4$ kg and radius $0.25$ m spins at $6$ rad/s about its symmetry axis. What is its angular momentum about that axis?
questions.why: $I=\tfrac12(4)(0.25)^2=0.125$ kg m², so $L=I\omega=0.75$. The wrong choices come from $MR^2\omega$ (treating all the mass as if it were on the rim), $\tfrac12MR\omega$ (forgetting to square $R$), and $\tfrac12I\omega^2$, which is the kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Same setup (1 kg ball, 1 m from the origin, $\omega = 2$ rad/s about $z$, rod in the $xz$-plane), but the rod now makes $60^\circ$ with the $z$ axis. What angle does the ball's $\mathbf L$ about the origin make with the $+z$ axis?
questions.why: $\mathbf r=(0.87,0,0.5)$ and $\mathbf v=1.73\,\hat{\mathbf y}$, so $\mathbf L=(-0.87,0,1.5)$, which is $30^\circ$ from $z$ and perpendicular to the rod. The wrong choices come from assuming $\mathbf L\parallel\boldsymbol\omega$, assuming $\mathbf L$ lies along the rod, and computing $\mathbf v\times\mathbf r$ (reversed order).

questions.stem: Two 0.5 kg balls sit at the ends of a massless rod, each 2 m from the center at the origin. The rod is tilted $30^\circ$ from the $z$ axis and spins about $z$ at 3 rad/s. What is the total $\mathbf L$?
choices: 6 kg m²/s, at 60° from the z axis
3 kg m²/s, along the z axis
12 kg m²/s, at 60° from the z axis
6 kg m²/s, along the z axis
questions.why: Each ball has $|\mathbf L|=mr^2\omega\sin30^\circ=3$, and the two point the same way (perpendicular to the rod), so the total is 6 at $60^\circ$ from $z$. The wrong choices come from assuming the sideways parts cancel (keeping only $L_z$), using $v=\omega r$ instead of $\omega r\sin\theta$, or assuming $\mathbf L\parallel\boldsymbol\omega$.

questions.stem: Two 1 kg balls sit at $\pm(0.6,\,0,\,0.8)$ m on a massless rod through the origin, which spins with $\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,5)$ rad/s. Using the inertia tensor about the origin, what is $\mathbf L$ (in kg m²/s)?
questions.why: $I_{xz}=-2(0.6)(0.8)=-0.96$ and $I_{zz}=2(0.36)=0.72$ kg m², so $\mathbf L=(-4.8,0,3.6)$. The wrong choices drop the minus sign on $I_{xz}$, use $x^2+y^2+z^2$ for $I_{zz}$, or ignore the off-diagonal entry.

questions.stem: The same dumbbell (moment 0 along the rod, $I_\perp=2$ kg m²) is now tilted $60^\circ$ from the $z$ axis and spins at $\boldsymbol\omega=3\hat{\mathbf z}$ rad/s. What is $\mathbf L$?
choices: 3√3 ≈ 5.2 kg m²/s, perpendicular to the rod (30° from z)
3 kg m²/s, perpendicular to the rod
questions.why: $\omega_\perp=3\sin60^\circ=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, so $L=I_\perp\omega_\perp=3\sqrt3$ along $\hat{\mathbf e}_\perp$. The wrong choices come from writing $\mathbf L=I_\perp\boldsymbol\omega$, using the along-rod component $\omega\cos60^\circ$, or treating all of $\boldsymbol\omega$ as lying along the rod.

questions.stem: A wheel spins at 6 rad/s relative to its horizontal axle while the axle turns about the vertical at 8 rad/s. What is the wheel's total angular velocity?
questions.why: $|\boldsymbol\omega|=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ rad/s, and $\tan\alpha=8/6$ gives $53^\circ$ above horizontal. The wrong choices add the speeds as scalars, invert the tangent, or ignore the axle's turning.

questions.stem: A spin angular momentum $\mathbf L=4\hat{\mathbf y}$ kg m²/s is carried around the vertical at $\boldsymbol\Omega=3\hat{\mathbf z}$ rad/s (counterclockwise seen from above). Its length stays the same. What is $d\mathbf L/dt$?
choices: $0$, because the length of $\mathbf L$ doesn't change
questions.why: $3\hat{\mathbf z}\times4\hat{\mathbf y}=-12\hat{\mathbf x}$. The answer $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ comes from reversing the order to $\mathbf L\times\boldsymbol\Omega$. The answer $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ assumes $\mathbf L$ gets longer. The answer 0 misses that $\mathbf L$ changes direction even though its length stays fixed.

questions.stem: The same gyroscope (mass 0.5 kg, $I_3=0.002$ kg m², axle 0.1 m from the pivot, $g=9.8$ m/s²) is now spun at 400 rad/s. Use the fast-spin approximation. What is its precession rate $\Omega$?
questions.why: $\Omega=Mg\ell/(I_3\omega_3)=0.49/0.8\approx0.61$ rad/s, so doubling the spin halves the precession rate. 2.45 assumes faster spin means faster precession. 1.63 inverts the formula to $L/\tau$. 6.1 leaves out the lever arm $\ell$.

questions.stem: A uniform stick of length $\ell=0.15$ m is pivoted at its top end. It swings steadily around the vertical at $\theta=60^\circ$ from the vertical. Take $g=9.8$ m/s². What is its angular frequency $\omega$?
questions.why: $\omega^2=3g/(2\ell\cos\theta)=29.4/0.15=196$, so $\omega=14$ rad/s. 11.4 uses the point-mass result $\sqrt{g/(\ell\cos\theta)}$. 9.9 uses the full $L$ instead of $L\cos\theta$. 19.8 puts gravity at the end of the stick instead of at the center of mass.

questions.stem: Same rolling wheel on a pivoted horizontal axle, now with $r=0.1$ m, $R=0.4$ m and $\Omega=3$ rad/s. What is the wheel's spin rate $\omega'$ relative to the axle?
questions.why: No slipping means $\omega' r=\Omega R$, so $\omega'=(0.4/0.1)(3)=12$ rad/s. The value 0.75 inverts $R/r$, 12.4 is the total $|\boldsymbol\omega|$ including $\Omega$, and 1.2 is the center's speed $\Omega R$.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass $2$ kg and radius $r=0.1$ m rolls on a pivoted horizontal axle as in rung 12, with $R=0.2$ m and $\Omega=3$ rad/s (so $\omega'=6$ rad/s). What is the vertical component $L_z$ of its angular momentum about the pivot?
questions.why: $L_z=I_\perp\Omega=(\tfrac14 mr^2+mR^2)\Omega=0.085\times3=0.255$ kg m²/s. Zero forgets that the axle turns, 0.015 leaves out the parallel-axis term $mR^2$, and 0.57 multiplies $I_\perp$ by $|\boldsymbol\omega|$ as if $\mathbf L=I\boldsymbol\omega$.

questions.stem: Same rolling disk ($m=2$ kg, $r=0.1$ m, massless axle, no horizontal force from the ground), now with $R=0.2$ m and $\Omega=3$ rad/s, so $\omega'=6$ rad/s. What is the normal force $N$? ($g=9.8$ m/s²)
questions.why: $N=mg+\Omega I_3\omega'/R=19.6+(3)(0.01)(6)/0.2=20.5$ N. 19.6 N ignores $d\mathbf L/dt$, 18.7 N has its sign flipped, and 23.5 N uses $\Omega|\mathbf L|$ instead of $\Omega L_\perp$.

questions.stem: A free symmetric body has $I_1=I_2=I=3$ kg m², $I_3=5$ kg m², and spins with $\omega_3=6$ rad/s plus a small sideways $\boldsymbol\omega$ component. Seen in the body frame, at what rate does $\boldsymbol\omega$ circle the symmetry axis?
questions.why: $\Omega=(I_3-I)\omega_3/I=(5-3)(6)/3=4$ rad/s. The wrong choices come from dividing by $I_3$ instead of $I$ (2.4), using the fixed-frame rate $L/I\approx I_3\omega_3/I$ (10), or wrongly arguing that $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\omega=0$ (0).

questions.stem: The same top ($I=0.01$ kg m², $I_3=0.004$ kg m², $\theta=60^\circ$) now has $Mg\ell=0.18$ J and spins with $\omega_3=25$ rad/s. What is its slow steady precession rate?
questions.why: Dividing $I\Omega^2\cos\theta-I_3\omega_3\Omega+Mg\ell=0$ by $I\cos\theta=0.005$ gives $\Omega^2-20\Omega+36=0$, so $\Omega=(20-\sqrt{256})/2=2$ rad/s. The fast-spin estimate $Mg\ell/(I_3\omega_3)$ gives 1.8, the other root is 18, and forgetting to halve gives 4.

questions.why: $I=0.5$ kg m² and $\tau=1$ N m, so $\alpha=\tau/I=2$ rad/s².

questions.stem: A particle has initial position $x_0$ (m), velocity $v_0$ (m/s) and constant acceleration $a$ (m/s$^2$). Which expression is dimensionally allowed for its position after time $t$?
questions.why: Every added term must have dimensions of length. Both $v_0t$ and $at^2$ are lengths. Units permit any dimensionless coefficient on $at^2$; they do not determine the correct coefficient $1/2$.

questions.stem: Newtonian gravity has force magnitude $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$. Given $[F]=ML/T^2$, what are the dimensions of $G$?
questions.why: $[G]=[F][r]^2/([m_1][m_2])=(ML/T^2)L^2/M^2=L^3/(MT^2)$. This is how the dimensions of a physical constant follow from a force law.

questions.stem: An ideal pendulum has bob mass $m$, length $\ell$ and gravitational acceleration $g$. At a fixed amplitude angle, write its angular frequency as $\omega=Cm^a\ell^bg^c$, where $C$ is dimensionless. Which powers give $[\omega]=1/T$?
questions.why: Mass gives $a=0$, length gives $b+c=0$, and time gives $-2c=-1$. Hence $\omega=C\sqrt{g/\ell}$. The result cannot depend on the sole mass, but $C$ may depend on the fixed dimensionless amplitude.

questions.stem: A linear spring has stiffness $k$ with dimensions $M/T^2$ and maximum displacement $A$ with dimensions $L$. Its oscillation energy depends only on $m,k,A$. Which expression has the required energy dimensions $ML^2/T^2$?
questions.why: Write $E=Cm^ak^bA^c$. Time requires $b=1$, mass then requires $a=0$, and length requires $c=2$. Thus $E=CkA^2$; dimensions alone cannot supply $C=1/2$.

questions.stem: A satellite just above a spherical planet has speed set only by surface gravity $g$ and planet radius $R$. If $g$ becomes $g/4$ and $R$ becomes $9R$, with the same dimensionless orbit conditions, what is the speed ratio $v_{new}/v_{old}$?
questions.why: The length and time powers give $v=C\sqrt{gR}$, so $v_{new}/v_{old}=\sqrt{(1/4)9}=3/2$. The unknown common constant cancels.

questions.stem: A negligible-mass satellite has an orbital time scale built only from radius $r$ and $\mu=GM$, where $[\mu]=L^3/T^2$. For $T_{orbit}=Cr^a\mu^b$, which powers have dimensions of time?
questions.why: Matching time gives $-2b=1$, and matching length gives $a+3b=0$. Thus $T_{orbit}=C\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}$. Dynamics and orbit shape determine the remaining dimensionless factor.

questions.stem: A pendulum has length $\ell$, gravity $g$ and maximum angle $\theta_0$ in radians. Which claim follows from dimensional analysis alone?
choices: $\omega$ must be proportional to the bob mass
questions.why: Angles in radians are dimensionless. An arbitrary function of $\theta_0$ changes no units, so dimensions cannot rule out amplitude dependence or determine a numerical coefficient. Dynamics supplies that information.

questions.stem: A spring obeys $F=-kx+bx^2$, where $[k]=M/T^2$ and $[b]=M/(LT^2)$. With amplitude $A$, which dimensionless parameter can alter its frequency from the linear-spring scale $\sqrt{k/m}$?
questions.why: $[bA]=M/T^2=[k]$, so $bA/k$ is dimensionless and $\omega=f(bA/k)\sqrt{k/m}$ is allowed. In contrast, for a perfectly linear spring with no other relevant length, $A$ cannot enter a dimensionless ratio.

questions.stem: Two proposed pendulum energies above the lowest point are $E_1=mg\ell$ and $E_2=mg\ell(1-\cos\theta_0)$. Which judgment can a units check alone make?
choices: Both have energy units; dimensions alone cannot choose their angle dependence
Only $E_1$ has energy units because angles cannot appear
Only $E_2$ has energy units because cosine supplies length
Both have force units rather than energy units
questions.why: $[mg\ell]=ML^2/T^2$ and $1-\cos\theta_0$ is dimensionless. Both pass units. Physical reasoning at zero amplitude rejects $E_1$ for this reference energy; that extra reasoning is not a units test.

questions.stem: A puck slides east at 3 m/s on level frictionless ice in an inertial frame. After the push ends, its horizontal net force is zero. What happens?
choices: It slows at a constant rate
questions.why: $\mathbf F_{net}=0$ implies $\mathbf a=0$, so velocity stays constant. Motion does not require a continuing force; changing velocity does.

questions.stem: A freely floating particle has constant velocity in an inertial laboratory. A camera accelerates east relative to that laboratory. The particle appears to accelerate west in the camera frame. What does this show?
choices: The camera frame is noninertial; apparent acceleration need not come from a real westward force
The particle must have gained a real westward interaction
Any frame where a camera is at rest is inertial
The laboratory is noninertial because the particle is moving
questions.why: An inertial frame makes every free particle move with constant velocity. Subtracting the accelerating camera motion introduces apparent acceleration; using Newton laws there requires inertial-force bookkeeping.

questions.stem: A ball thrown straight upward reaches its highest point in an inertial frame. Neglect air resistance. At that instant, which statement is correct?
choices: Its velocity is zero but its acceleration is $g$ downward
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Its velocity is zero and acceleration is $g$ upward
Zero velocity means no gravitational force acts
questions.why: Gravity remains $mg$ downward throughout the flight. The instantaneous zero velocity is not constant velocity over a time interval, so it does not imply zero force or acceleration.

questions.stem: For the same fixed collection of Newtonian particles in an inertial frame, which statement correctly relates net external force, total momentum and acceleration?
choices: $\sum\mathbf F_{ext}=d\mathbf p/dt$; for one constant-mass particle this becomes $m\mathbf a$
$\sum\mathbf F_{ext}=\mathbf p$; force keeps velocity nonzero
$d\mathbf p/dt=m\mathbf a$ even when the particle mass changes
questions.why: Force is a rate of change of momentum, not momentum or velocity. Differentiating $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$ gives $m\mathbf a$ when mass is constant. Changing-mass systems require careful system-boundary accounting.

questions.stem: The same net force acts separately on masses $m$ and $3m$ in an inertial frame. Their acceleration magnitudes are $a_1$ and $a_2$. What is $a_1/a_2$?
questions.why: $a_1=F/m$ and $a_2=F/(3m)$, so the ratio is 3. This inverse-mass relation is observable and distinguishes $F=ma$ from an arbitrary invented quantity such as $m^2a$.

questions.stem: A 2 kg particle has velocity $\mathbf v=(4,0)$ m/s and net force $\mathbf F=(-6,8)$ N in an inertial frame. What is its acceleration?
questions.why: Apply $a_x=F_x/m=-3$ and $a_y=F_y/m=4$. Acceleration follows net force, not the current velocity: the particle initially slows in x while acquiring y velocity.

questions.stem: When should the constant-mass Newtonian relation $\mathbf F_{net}=m\mathbf a$ be treated as the appropriate approximation?
choices: For ordinary macroscopic motion at speeds much smaller than light speed, measured in an inertial frame
For any particle at any speed without changing the momentum law
Only when the particle is at rest
Only when gravity is the sole force
questions.why: Newtonian mechanics describes ordinary low-speed macroscopic motion very well. Relativistic speeds or quantum-scale behavior can require other theories. Neither rest nor a gravity-only force is required.

questions.stem: A book rests on a horizontal table. What is the third-law partner of the gravitational force Earth exerts on the book?
choices: The gravitational force the book exerts on Earth
The upward contact force the table exerts on the book
The contact force the book exerts on the table
The sum of all forces on the book
questions.why: A third-law pair belongs to the same interaction with source and receiving bodies exchanged. Earth pulls the book downward and the book pulls Earth toward it. The normal force is a different interaction, even when its magnitude equals the weight.

questions.stem: Two initially resting carts of masses $m$ and $3m$ push apart through an internal spring on a frictionless horizontal track. There is no external horizontal force. Which statement holds during the push?
choices: Their horizontal momenta sum to zero, while the lighter cart has three times the acceleration magnitude
Their accelerations have equal magnitudes because their interaction forces are equal
The heavier cart exerts three times the force on the lighter cart
Their total horizontal momentum increases as the spring releases
questions.why: The internal forces are equal and opposite. Separately, $a=F/m$, so the lighter cart accelerates three times as much. Adding the momentum-rate equations cancels internal forces, keeping total horizontal momentum at its initial zero value.

questions.stem: Two isolated particles interact only through an ordinary equal-and-opposite mechanical force. Which equation explains conservation of their total momentum?
choices: $\mathbf p_1=\mathbf p_2$ because the forces are equal in magnitude
$\mathbf a_1=\mathbf a_2$ even when the masses differ
questions.why: Each momentum derivative equals the force on that particle. Summing adds the pair; the third law makes their vector sum zero. Conservation fixes the total momentum, not equal individual momenta or accelerations.

questions.stem: Is the statement "two particles always exert equal-and-opposite instantaneous forces on one another" an unrestricted law for electromagnetic interactions too?
choices: No; electromagnetic fields can carry momentum, so particle momentum alone need not be conserved
Yes; momentum can never reside outside particles
No; this means total momentum including fields cannot be conserved
Yes; equal masses are enough to guarantee it for any interaction
questions.why: The mechanical particle model used here assumes third-law force pairs. For electromagnetic interactions, fields can carry momentum; momentum conservation must include particles and fields. This limits the particle-only statement without abandoning total momentum conservation.

questions.stem: An ideal spring obeys $F=-kx$. Its only relevant dimensionful ingredients are mass $m$, stiffness $k$ and amplitude $A$. If its period is $P=Cm^ak^bA^c$, which exponents give dimensions of time?
questions.why: Because $[k]=M/T^2$, the product has dimensions $M^{a+b}T^{-2b}L^c$. Thus $a+b=0$, $-2b=1$, and $c=0$: $P=C\sqrt{m/k}$, independent of amplitude under these assumptions. Dynamics, not dimensions, gives $C=2\pi$.
